claim: Bovines have evolved a subset of antibodies with ultra-long heavy chain complementarity determining regions that harbour cysteine-rich knob domains.
source: Bovines have evolved a subset of antibodies with ultra-long heavy chain complementarity determining regions that harbour cysteine-rich knob domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about bovine antibodies.

claim: Autonomous 3–6 kDa knob domains were previously isolated from bovine antibodies.
source: To produce high-affinity peptides, we previously isolated autonomous 3–6 kDa knob domains from bovine antibodies.
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors, as indicated by 'previously isolated'.

claim: Four knob domain peptides elicit a range of effects on complement C5.
source: Here, we show that binding of four knob domain peptides elicits a range of effects on the clinically validated drug target complement C5.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Allosteric mechanisms predominated in the effects of knob domain peptides on C5.
source: Allosteric mechanisms predominated, with one peptide selectively inhibiting C5 cleavage by the alternative pathway C5 convertase, revealing a targetable mechanistic difference between the classical and alternative pathway C5 convertases.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by functional assays and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One peptide selectively inhibits C5 cleavage by the alternative pathway C5 convertase.
source: Allosteric mechanisms predominated, with one peptide selectively inhibiting C5 cleavage by the alternative pathway C5 convertase, revealing a targetable mechanistic difference between the classical and alternative pathway C5 convertases.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays showing pathway-specific inhibition.

claim: There is a targetable mechanistic difference between the classical and alternative pathway C5 convertases.
source: Allosteric mechanisms predominated, with one peptide selectively inhibiting C5 cleavage by the alternative pathway C5 convertase, revealing a targetable mechanistic difference between the classical and alternative pathway C5 convertases.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective inhibition observed with K92 peptide.

claim: C5-knob domain co-crystal structures were determined.
source: Taking a hybrid biophysical approach, we present C5-knob domain co-crystal structures and, by solution methods, observed allosteric effects propagating >50 Å from the binding sites.
evidence: Crystal structures are presented in the manuscript with PDB accession codes.

claim: Allosteric effects propagate more than 50 Å from the binding sites.
source: Taking a hybrid biophysical approach, we present C5-knob domain co-crystal structures and, by solution methods, observed allosteric effects propagating >50 Å from the binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS and SAXS data showing conformational changes distant from the binding site.

claim: By the end of 2019, over 60 peptide drugs have received regulatory approval.
source: By the end of 2019, over 60 peptide drugs have received regulatory approval, with an estimated 400 more in active development globally (Lau and Dunn, 2018; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An estimated 400 peptide drugs are in active development globally.
source: By the end of 2019, over 60 peptide drugs have received regulatory approval, with an estimated 400 more in active development globally (Lau and Dunn, 2018; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A method for deriving peptides from the ultra-long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 was previously reported.
source: As a potential route to discover therapeutic peptides, we previously reported a method for deriving peptides from the ultra-long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 (ul-CDRH3), which are unique to a subset of bovine antibodies (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors with a citation.

claim: Ultra-long CDRH3 are unique to a subset of bovine antibodies.
source: As a potential route to discover therapeutic peptides, we previously reported a method for deriving peptides from the ultra-long heavy chain complementarity determining region 3 (ul-CDRH3), which are unique to a subset of bovine antibodies (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bovine antibodies, supported by citation.

claim: Knob domains can bind antigen autonomously when removed from the antibody scaffold.
source: We have shown that knob domains, a cysteine-rich mini-domain common to all ul-CDRH3, can bind antigen autonomously when removed from the antibody scaffold (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Knob domains are a cysteine-rich mini-domain common to all ul-CDRH3.
source: We have shown that knob domains, a cysteine-rich mini-domain common to all ul-CDRH3, can bind antigen autonomously when removed from the antibody scaffold (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about knob domains, supported by citation.

claim: Peptide affinity maturation can be performed in vivo using the cow's immune system.
source: This allows peptide affinity maturation to be performed in vivo, harnessing the cow's immune system to produce peptides with complex stabilising networks of disulphide bonds.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the approach described.

claim: The cow's immune system produces peptides with complex stabilising networks of disulphide bonds.
source: This allows peptide affinity maturation to be performed in vivo, harnessing the cow's immune system to produce peptides with complex stabilising networks of disulphide bonds.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing disulphide bonds in the knob domains.

claim: The discovery method for knob domain peptides involves immunisation of cattle followed by cell sorting of B-cells using fluorescently labelled antigen.
source: For the discovery of knob domain peptides, immunisation of cattle is followed by cell sorting of B-cells using fluorescently labelled antigen.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the discovery process.

claim: A library of antigen-specific CDRH3 sequences is created by performing RT PCR on B-cell lysate.
source: A library of antigen-specific CDRH3 sequences is created by performing a reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT PCR) on the B-cell lysate, followed by a PCR using primers specific to the conserved framework regions which flank CDRH3 (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ultra-long CDRH3s are immediately evident upon sequencing.
source: Upon sequencing, ul-CDRH3s are immediately evident and the knob domains can be expressed recombinantly as cleavable fusion proteins (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological observation supported by citation.

claim: Knob domains can be expressed recombinantly as cleavable fusion proteins.
source: Upon sequencing, ul-CDRH3s are immediately evident and the knob domains can be expressed recombinantly as cleavable fusion proteins (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by citation and used in the current study.

claim: The method for discovery of knob domain peptides was established using complement component C5.
source: This method for the discovery of knob domain peptides was established using complement component C5, and we reported peptides which bound C5 with affinities in the pM–low nM range (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to prior work establishing the method, supported by citation.

claim: Peptides were reported that bound C5 with affinities in the pM–low nM range.
source: This method for the discovery of knob domain peptides was established using complement component C5, and we reported peptides which bound C5 with affinities in the pM–low nM range (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: C5 is the target of effective therapies for diseases with pathogenic complement dysregulation.
source: C5 is the éminence grise of the complement cascade's druggable proteins, and the target of effective therapies for diseases with pathogenic complement dysregulation, of which paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (Rother et al., 2007) and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (Nürnberger et al., 2009) are notable examples.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a disease with pathogenic complement dysregulation.
source: C5 is the éminence grise of the complement cascade's druggable proteins, and the target of effective therapies for diseases with pathogenic complement dysregulation, of which paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (Rother et al., 2007) and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (Nürnberger et al., 2009) are notable examples.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a disease with pathogenic complement dysregulation.
source: C5 is the éminence grise of the complement cascade's druggable proteins, and the target of effective therapies for diseases with pathogenic complement dysregulation, of which paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (Rother et al., 2007) and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (Nürnberger et al., 2009) are notable examples.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Six monoclonal antibodies targeting C5 have reached, or are entering, clinical trials.
source: Six monoclonal antibodies targeting C5 have reached, or are entering, clinical trials, closely followed by C5-targeting immune evasion molecules (Romay-Penabad et al., 2014), aptamers (Biesecker et al., 1999), cyclic peptides (Ricardo et al., 2014), interfering RNA (Borodovsky et al., 2014), and small molecules (Jendza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the therapeutic landscape, supported by citations.

claim: C5 inhibitors are being trialled for the treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome arising from SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Currently, C5 inhibitors are being trialled for the treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome arising from severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection (Smith et al., 2020; Wilkinson et al., 2020; Zelek et al., 2020) and for the neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis (Albazli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is current clinical information supported by citations.

claim: C5 inhibitors are being trialled for the treatment of myasthenia gravis.
source: Currently, C5 inhibitors are being trialled for the treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome arising from severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection (Smith et al., 2020; Wilkinson et al., 2020; Zelek et al., 2020) and for the neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis (Albazli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is current clinical information supported by citation.

claim: C5 is the principal effector of the terminal portion of the complement cascade.
source: C5 is the principal effector of the terminal portion of the complement cascade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complement system.

claim: C5 is cleaved into two moieties with distinct biological functions at high local C3b concentrations.
source: At high local C3b concentrations, arising from activation of either or both of the classical (CP) and mannose binding lectin (LP) pathways, aided by the amplificatory alternative pathway (AP), C5 is cleaved into two moieties with distinct biological functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement activation.

claim: C5 cleavage is performed by two convertases: C4bC2aC3b and C3bBbC3b.
source: Cleavage is performed by two convertases: C4bC2aC3b, formed in response to CP or LP activation (Takata et al., 1987) (henceforth the CP C5 convertase), and C3bBbC3b, formed in response to AP activation (DiScipio, 1981) (henceforth the AP C5 convertase).
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement convertases, supported by citations.

claim: The CP and AP C5 convertases are thought to be mechanistically identical.
source: Although the constitutive components of the C5 convertases differ, they are thought to be mechanistically identical.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field that the current study challenges.

claim: C5a is the most proinflammatory anaphylatoxin derived from the complement cascade.
source: Once cleaved, the C5a fragment is the most proinflammatory anaphylatoxin derived from the complement cascade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement biology.

claim: C5a signals through C5aR1 and C5aR2.
source: When signalling through C5aR1 and C5aR2, C5a is a strong chemoattractant recruiting neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and T lymphocytes to sites of complement activation, whereupon it activates phagocytic cells, prompting degranulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C5a signaling.

claim: C5a is a strong chemoattractant recruiting neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and T lymphocytes to sites of complement activation.
source: When signalling through C5aR1 and C5aR2, C5a is a strong chemoattractant recruiting neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and T lymphocytes to sites of complement activation, whereupon it activates phagocytic cells, prompting degranulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C5a function.

claim: C5b interacts with C6, recruiting C7–C9 to form the terminal C5b-9 complement complex.
source: C5b, meanwhile, interacts with C6, recruiting C7–C9 to form the terminal C5b-9 complement complex or TCC (Lachmann and Thompson, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement cascade, supported by citation.

claim: The TCC is referred to as the membrane attack complex (MAC) when inserted into a cell membrane.
source: Once inserted into a cell membrane, the TCC is referred to as the membrane attack complex (MAC), a membrane-spanning pore which can lyse sensitive cells (Götze and Müller-Eberhard, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement biology, supported by citation.

claim: The MAC is a membrane-spanning pore which can lyse sensitive cells.
source: Once inserted into a cell membrane, the TCC is referred to as the membrane attack complex (MAC), a membrane-spanning pore which can lyse sensitive cells (Götze and Müller-Eberhard, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAC function, supported by citation.

claim: A crystal structure of apo C5 has been determined.
source: Aspects of the structural biology of C5 are well understood due to a crystal structure of the apo form (Fredslund et al., 2008) and a number of co-crystal structures of C5 with various modulators.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Co-crystal structures of C5 with various modulators have been determined.
source: Aspects of the structural biology of C5 are well understood due to a crystal structure of the apo form (Fredslund et al., 2008) and a number of co-crystal structures of C5 with various modulators.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by subsequent citations.

claim: SSL-7 is an inhibitory molecule derived from Staphylococcus aureus.
source: By virtue of its constitutive role in the terminal pathway, C5 is a recurrent target for immune evasion molecules and structures have been determined of C5 in complex with an inhibitory molecule derived from Staphylococcus aureus, SSL-7 (Laursen et al., 2010), as well as several structurally distinct examples from ticks: OmCI (Jore et al., 2016), RaCI (Jore et al., 2016), and Cirp-T (Reichhardt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: OmCI, RaCI, and Cirp-T are structurally distinct immune evasion molecules from ticks.
source: By virtue of its constitutive role in the terminal pathway, C5 is a recurrent target for immune evasion molecules and structures have been determined of C5 in complex with an inhibitory molecule derived from Staphylococcus aureus, SSL-7 (Laursen et al., 2010), as well as several structurally distinct examples from ticks: OmCI (Jore et al., 2016), RaCI (Jore et al., 2016), and Cirp-T (Reichhardt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The structure of C5 with the inhibitory monoclonal antibody eculizumab has been determined.
source: Additionally, the structures of C5 with the inhibitory monoclonal antibody (mAb) eculizumab (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016), of C5 with a small molecule inhibitor (Jendza et al., 2019), and of C5 with the complement-depleting agent cobra venom factor (CVF) (Laursen et al., 2011) have all been determined.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The structure of C5 with a small molecule inhibitor has been determined.
source: Additionally, the structures of C5 with the inhibitory monoclonal antibody (mAb) eculizumab (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016), of C5 with a small molecule inhibitor (Jendza et al., 2019), and of C5 with the complement-depleting agent cobra venom factor (CVF) (Laursen et al., 2011) have all been determined.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The structure of C5 with cobra venom factor has been determined.
source: Additionally, the structures of C5 with the inhibitory monoclonal antibody (mAb) eculizumab (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016), of C5 with a small molecule inhibitor (Jendza et al., 2019), and of C5 with the complement-depleting agent cobra venom factor (CVF) (Laursen et al., 2011) have all been determined.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: K8 has an equilibrium dissociation constant of 17.8 nM for human C5.
source: Previously we reported equilibrium dissociation constants of 17.8 nM for K8, 1.4 nM for K57, <0.6 nM for K92, and 15.5 nM for K149 (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: K57 has an equilibrium dissociation constant of 1.4 nM for human C5.
source: Previously we reported equilibrium dissociation constants of 17.8 nM for K8, 1.4 nM for K57, <0.6 nM for K92, and 15.5 nM for K149 (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: K92 has an equilibrium dissociation constant of less than 0.6 nM for human C5.
source: Previously we reported equilibrium dissociation constants of 17.8 nM for K8, 1.4 nM for K57, <0.6 nM for K92, and 15.5 nM for K149 (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: K149 has an equilibrium dissociation constant of 15.5 nM for human C5.
source: Previously we reported equilibrium dissociation constants of 17.8 nM for K8, 1.4 nM for K57, <0.6 nM for K92, and 15.5 nM for K149 (Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: K57 is a potent and fully efficacious inhibitor of C5 activation.
source: Here, we show that K57 was a potent and fully efficacious inhibitor of C5 activation, preventing release of C5a, and deposition of C5b and C9.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: K57 prevents release of C5a and deposition of C5b and C9.
source: Here, we show that K57 was a potent and fully efficacious inhibitor of C5 activation, preventing release of C5a, and deposition of C5b and C9.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K57 has no effect on C3b, which is upstream of C5.
source: As expected, there was no effect on C3b, which is upstream of C5 (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K149 is a high-affinity silent binder with no discernible effect on C5a release, formation of C5b neo-epitope or C9 deposition.
source: In contrast, K149 was a high-affinity silent binder with no discernible effect on C5a release, formation of C5b neo-epitope or C9 deposition, even at peptide concentrations in excess of 100 × KD (see Supplementary file 1 Section 1).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data.

claim: K8 and K92 exerted allosteric effects on C5.
source: K8 and K92 exerted more nuanced allosteric effects on C5 (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data and structural analysis.

claim: K92 partially prevented C5 activation by the AP.
source: By ELISA, K92 partially prevented C5 activation by the AP, but, intriguingly, no effect was observed in CP assays, suggesting K92 selectively inhibits C5 activation by the AP C5 convertase, but not the CP C5 convertase.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K92 selectively inhibits C5 activation by the AP C5 convertase, but not the CP C5 convertase.
source: By ELISA, K92 partially prevented C5 activation by the AP, but, intriguingly, no effect was observed in CP assays, suggesting K92 selectively inhibits C5 activation by the AP C5 convertase, but not the CP C5 convertase.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects in AP vs CP assays.

claim: Partial antagonists with Emax below 100% are an impossible mode of pharmacology for orthosteric antagonists.
source: Partial antagonists, where the degree of inhibition for the asymptotic concentrations of a dose–response curve (Emax) is below 100%, are an impossible mode of pharmacology for orthosteric antagonists (Klein et al., 2013), and we therefore propose that K92 operates by a non-steric mechanism.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: K92 operates by a non-steric mechanism.
source: Partial antagonists, where the degree of inhibition for the asymptotic concentrations of a dose–response curve (Emax) is below 100%, are an impossible mode of pharmacology for orthosteric antagonists (Klein et al., 2013), and we therefore propose that K92 operates by a non-steric mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial antagonist behavior and pharmacological principles.

claim: K8 partially inhibited both the AP and CP.
source: K8 was also demonstrably allosteric, partially inhibiting both the AP and CP in ELISA experiments.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K8 and K92 have no effect on C3b deposition.
source: For K8 and K92, no effect on C3b deposition was detected.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K57 is a potent and fully efficacious inhibitor of complement-mediated cell lysis in CP and AP haemolysis assays.
source: When tested in CP and AP haemolysis assays (Figure 1E, F), K57 was a potent and fully efficacious inhibitor of complement-mediated cell lysis.
evidence: This is supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K92 was active solely in the AP-driven haemolysis assay, achieving Emax values of 30–40%.
source: Consistent with the ELISA data, K92 was active solely in the AP-driven haemolysis assay, achieving Emax values of 30–40%; while K8 was efficacious in the CP assay but did not show activity in the AP assay below 10 µM, potentially a consequence of the increased serum concentration and stringency of the haemolysis endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: K8 was efficacious in the CP haemolysis assay but did not show activity in the AP assay below 10 µM.
source: Consistent with the ELISA data, K92 was active solely in the AP-driven haemolysis assay, achieving Emax values of 30–40%; while K8 was efficacious in the CP assay but did not show activity in the AP assay below 10 µM, potentially a consequence of the increased serum concentration and stringency of the haemolysis endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Saturation of C5 with K8 entirely prevented binding of K92.
source: We detected negative cooperativity between K8 and K92, whereby saturation of C5 with K8 entirely prevented binding of K92.
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When C5 is saturated with K92, K8 can still bind, albeit to a lesser degree.
source: When the order of addition was changed and C5 was saturated with K92, K8 was still able to bind, albeit to a lesser degree (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Saturation of C5 with K8 entirely eliminated binding of K57.
source: Saturation of C5 with K8 also entirely eliminated binding of K57, with a similar order of addition effect, whereby K8 could still partially bind to the C5-K57 complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: K8 could still partially bind to the C5-K57 complex.
source: Saturation of C5 with K8 also entirely eliminated binding of K57, with a similar order of addition effect, whereby K8 could still partially bind to the C5-K57 complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When C5 is saturated with K92 or K57, only very small amounts of subsequent binding of either peptide were observed.
source: When C5 was saturated with K92 or K57, only very small amounts of subsequent binding of either peptide were observed by SPR (Figure 2C), suggesting that the epitopes do not overlap but that considerable negative cooperativity exists.
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The epitopes of K92 and K57 do not overlap but considerable negative cooperativity exists.
source: When C5 was saturated with K92 or K57, only very small amounts of subsequent binding of either peptide were observed by SPR (Figure 2C), suggesting that the epitopes do not overlap but that considerable negative cooperativity exists.
evidence: This is inferred from the SPR cross blocking data.

claim: Saturation of C5 with K8, K57, or K92 did not prevent subsequent binding of K149.
source: Saturation of C5 with K8, K57, or K92 did not prevent subsequent binding of the non-functional K149 (Figure 2D), suggesting K149 does not share an epitope with the other ligands, nor does it significantly perturb C5 such that the other binding sites are affected.
evidence: This is supported by SPR cross blocking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: K149 does not share an epitope with K8, K57, or K92.
source: Saturation of C5 with K8, K57, or K92 did not prevent subsequent binding of the non-functional K149 (Figure 2D), suggesting K149 does not share an epitope with the other ligands, nor does it significantly perturb C5 such that the other binding sites are affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the SPR cross blocking data.

claim: K149 does not significantly perturb C5 such that the other binding sites are affected.
source: Saturation of C5 with K8, K57, or K92 did not prevent subsequent binding of the non-functional K149 (Figure 2D), suggesting K149 does not share an epitope with the other ligands, nor does it significantly perturb C5 such that the other binding sites are affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the SPR cross blocking data.

claim: The crystal structure of the C5-K8 complex was determined at a resolution of 2.3 Å.
source: To elucidate the structural basis for the allosteric modulation of C5, we determined the crystal structure of the C5-K8 complex at a resolution of 2.3 Å (see Supplementary file 1, Table 2.1 for data collection and structure refinement statistics).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding of the study.

claim: K8 binds to the MG8 domain of the C5 α-chain.
source: The structure of the C5-K8 complex shows the K8 peptide binding to a previously unrecognised regulatory site on C5; the macroglobulin (MG) 8 domain of the α-chain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The K8 binding site on C5 is a previously unrecognised regulatory site.
source: The structure of the C5-K8 complex shows the K8 peptide binding to a previously unrecognised regulatory site on C5; the macroglobulin (MG) 8 domain of the α-chain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a novel finding from the crystal structure.

claim: K8 adopts a cysteine knot-like configuration with a flattened 3-strand β-sheet topology constrained by three disulphide bonds.
source: K8 adopts a cysteine knot-like configuration, where a flattened 3-strand β-sheet topology is constrained by three disulphide bonds (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The K8-C5 interaction surface has a total buried surface area of 1642 Å2.
source: Analysis of the K8-C5 complex with the macromolecular interfaces analysis tool PDBePISA (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) reveals a large interaction surface (total buried surface area in complex: 1642 Å2; with 852 Å2 contributed by K8 and 790 Å2 by C5), comparable to those seen in Fab-antigen complexes (Ramaraj et al., 2012), stabilised by an extensive network of 18 hydrogen bonds between K8 and the MG8 domain (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1), dominated by arginine residues R23K8, R32K8, and R45K8.
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis using PDBePISA.

claim: The K8-C5 interaction is stabilised by an extensive network of 18 hydrogen bonds.
source: Analysis of the K8-C5 complex with the macromolecular interfaces analysis tool PDBePISA (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) reveals a large interaction surface (total buried surface area in complex: 1642 Å2; with 852 Å2 contributed by K8 and 790 Å2 by C5), comparable to those seen in Fab-antigen complexes (Ramaraj et al., 2012), stabilised by an extensive network of 18 hydrogen bonds between K8 and the MG8 domain (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1), dominated by arginine residues R23K8, R32K8, and R45K8.
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The K8-C5 hydrogen bond network is dominated by arginine residues R23K8, R32K8, and R45K8.
source: Analysis of the K8-C5 complex with the macromolecular interfaces analysis tool PDBePISA (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) reveals a large interaction surface (total buried surface area in complex: 1642 Å2; with 852 Å2 contributed by K8 and 790 Å2 by C5), comparable to those seen in Fab-antigen complexes (Ramaraj et al., 2012), stabilised by an extensive network of 18 hydrogen bonds between K8 and the MG8 domain (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1), dominated by arginine residues R23K8, R32K8, and R45K8.
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The K8-C5 interaction includes ionic interactions between R32K8 and D1471C5, D25K8 and K1409C5, and H36K8 and D1382C5.
source: The extensive H-bond network is further bolstered by several ionic interactions, between R32K8 and D1471C5 (C5 numbering based on mature sequence), D25K8 and K1409C5, and H36K8 and D1382C5 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1 Table 2.3).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of the C5-K92 complex was determined at a resolution of 2.75 Å.
source: We also present a crystal structure of the C5-K92 complex at a resolution of 2.75 Å (see Supplementary file 1 for data collection and structure refinement statistics).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding of the study.

claim: K92 binds between the MG1 and MG5 domains of the β-chain of C5.
source: Two extended loop regions interact with C5, including an α-helix containing loop between β-strands 1 and 2, occupying a cleft between the MG1 and MG5 domains of the β-chain of C5.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: K92 adopts a 3-strand β-sheet topology stapled with two disulphide bonds.
source: Similar to K8, K92 adopts a 3-strand β-sheet topology (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) but stapled with only two disulphide bonds.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and disulphide mapping.

claim: The K92-C5 interaction surface has a total buried surface area of 1365 Å2.
source: The interaction surface (total buried surface area: 1365 Å2; with 750 Å2 contributed by K92 and 615 Å2 by C5) is sustained via a sparse set of eight H-bonds (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.5).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The K92-C5 interaction is sustained via eight hydrogen bonds.
source: The interaction surface (total buried surface area: 1365 Å2; with 750 Å2 contributed by K92 and 615 Å2 by C5) is sustained via a sparse set of eight H-bonds (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.5).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: A series of π–π and aliphatic–aromatic stacking interactions spans K92, encompassing F26K92, H25K92, W21K92, W6K92, and P3K92.
source: A series of π–π and aliphatic–aromatic stacking interactions spans K92, encompassing F26K92, H25K92, W21K92, W6K92, and P3K92 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The K8 R23A mutant resulted in a modest twofold decrease in affinity.
source: For K8, the R23A resulted in modest twofold decrease in affinity, but R32A was markedly more attenuating, with a 715-fold drop in affinity (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.6).
evidence: This is supported by SPR kinetics data.

claim: The K8 R32A mutant resulted in a 715-fold drop in affinity.
source: For K8, the R23A resulted in modest twofold decrease in affinity, but R32A was markedly more attenuating, with a 715-fold drop in affinity (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.6).
evidence: This is supported by SPR kinetics data.

claim: The K92 W21A mutant resulted in a 1209.2-fold drop in affinity.
source: For K92, the loss of hydrophobic interactions with C5 in W21A and F26A mutants markedly abridged affinity with a 1209.2-fold and 45.7-fold drop in affinity, respectively (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.6).
evidence: This is supported by SPR kinetics data.

claim: The K92 F26A mutant resulted in a 45.7-fold drop in affinity.
source: For K92, the loss of hydrophobic interactions with C5 in W21A and F26A mutants markedly abridged affinity with a 1209.2-fold and 45.7-fold drop in affinity, respectively (Supplementary file 1, Table 2.6).
evidence: This is supported by SPR kinetics data.

claim: Binding pose metadynamics suggested that both K8 and K92's binding poses were exceptionally stable.
source: To analyse the interfaces observed in the structures, we performed binding pose metadynamics (Clark et al., 2016), an analysis typically employed to computationally evaluate the binding stability of chemical ligands (Fusani et al., 2020). This in silico analysis suggested that both K8 and K92's binding poses were exceptionally stable, with the interface maintaining the key interactions in spite of applied force (Supplementary file 1, Tables 2.7 and 2.8).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis.

claim: For K92, both the backbone amide and carbonyl of C23K92 participate in H-bonds with the side chain of S82C5.
source: For K92, both the backbone amide and carbonyl of C23K92 participate in H-bonds with the side chain of S82C5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: For K8, an interchain sulphur–π stack between the C27K8-C41K8 disulphide bond and the aromatic of Y1378C5 positions the hydroxyl group of Y1378C5 to make a H-bond with D25K8.
source: For K8, an interchain sulphur–π stack between the C27K8-C41K8 disulphide bond and the aromatic of Y1378C5 positions the hydroxyl group of Y1378C5 to make a H-bond with D25K8 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: For K92, an intra-chain sulphur–π stack between the C9K92-C23K92 disulphide bond and the aromatic of Y14K92 orientates Y14K92 such that its hydroxyl group participates in an interchain H-bond with N38C5.
source: While for K92, an intra-chain sulphur–π stack between the C9K92-C23K92 disulphide bond and the aromatic of Y14K92 orientates Y14K92, such that its hydroxyl group participates in an interchain H-bond with N38C5.
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: The paratopes of K8 and K92 contain 18 and 10 residues, respectively.
source: The paratopes of K8 and K92 contain 18 and 10 residues, respectively, which are within the typical range of antibody paratope sizes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis and comparison to antibody databases.

claim: K8 and K92 paratope sizes are within the typical range of antibody paratope sizes.
source: The paratopes of K8 and K92 contain 18 and 10 residues, respectively, which are within the typical range of antibody paratope sizes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is derived from comparison to a database of antibody structures.

claim: No structurally and physicochemically similar antibody paratopes to K8 and K92 were found in a database of 924 antibody complexes.
source: Given this similarity in size, we searched for structurally and physicochemically similar antibody paratopes from the 924 antibody complexes but no similar paratope sites were found (Wong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is derived from computational comparison to antibody databases.

claim: The presence of cysteine in knob domain paratopes is uncommon in most antibody paratopes.
source: In terms of residue usage, one difference in paratope composition that is potentially universal is the presence of cysteine in the knob domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) which is uncommon in most antibody paratopes, with the exception of the CDR1-CDR3 disulphides, which have been described in camelid VHH (Govaert et al., 2012), and in broadly neutralising antibodies; those which cross react with several strains of a virus, and for which a disulphide bond in CDRH3 has been described in antibodies against HIV-1 (Hutchinson et al., 2019) and hepatitis C (Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is derived from comparison to antibody databases and established knowledge.

claim: K8 has 15 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions.
source: Using Arpeggio (Jubb, 2015) to identify inter- (antigen contacting) and intra-paratope interactions (hydrogen bond, polar, ionic, and hydrophobic) revealed that, on average, antibodies have 16 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions; K8 is very close to this, with 15 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions, whereas K92 paratope has fewer, with 9 intra-paratope and 10 inter-paratope interactions.
evidence: This is derived from computational analysis of the structure.

claim: K92 has 9 intra-paratope and 10 inter-paratope interactions.
source: Using Arpeggio (Jubb, 2015) to identify inter- (antigen contacting) and intra-paratope interactions (hydrogen bond, polar, ionic, and hydrophobic) revealed that, on average, antibodies have 16 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions; K8 is very close to this, with 15 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions, whereas K92 paratope has fewer, with 9 intra-paratope and 10 inter-paratope interactions.
evidence: This is derived from computational analysis of the structure.

claim: On average, antibodies have 16 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions.
source: Using Arpeggio (Jubb, 2015) to identify inter- (antigen contacting) and intra-paratope interactions (hydrogen bond, polar, ionic, and hydrophobic) revealed that, on average, antibodies have 16 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions; K8 is very close to this, with 15 intra-paratope and 17 inter-paratope interactions, whereas K92 paratope has fewer, with 9 intra-paratope and 10 inter-paratope interactions.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of antibody database structures.

claim: A bovine Fab with an ul-CDRH3 was recently crystallised in complex with a soluble portion of the HIV envelope.
source: A bovine Fab with an ul-CDRH3 was recently crystallised in complex with antigen, in this case a soluble portion of the HIV envelope (Stanfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from recent literature, supported by citation.

claim: A search for structurally homologous proteins using DALI did not find any 3D structures similar to K8 or K92.
source: A search for structurally homologous proteins, using the DALI protein structure comparison server (Holm, 2020), did not find any 3D structures similar to K8 or K92, including the 14 known structures of bovine Fabs with ul-CDRH3 in the PDB.
evidence: This is derived from computational structural comparison.

claim: Cyclic peptides on average sustain eight electrostatic interactions with their protein target, with a range of 1–20.
source: A recent review summarised the interactions mediated by cyclic peptides bound to proteins, across 65 co-crystal structures in the PDB (Malde et al., 2019). This revealed that cyclic peptides on average sustain eight electrostatic interactions with their protein target, with a range of 1–20.
evidence: This is established knowledge from literature review, supported by citation.

claim: K8's 19 inter-paratope interactions are comparatively high for a peptide.
source: When we consider K8, its 19 inter-paratope interactions are comparatively high for a peptide, while the seven inter-paratope interactions of K92 are far more typical (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is derived from comparison to cyclic peptide literature.

claim: K92's seven inter-paratope interactions are typical for a peptide.
source: When we consider K8, its 19 inter-paratope interactions are comparatively high for a peptide, while the seven inter-paratope interactions of K92 are far more typical (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is derived from comparison to cyclic peptide literature.

claim: The epitope for K92 is entirely contained within the binding interface of SSL7.
source: When compared to the binding sites of other C5 modulators (Figure 4A), it can be observed that the epitope for K92 is entirely contained within the binding interface of a previously reported immune evasion molecule, the 23 kDa SSL7 protein from S. aureus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is derived from structural comparison.

claim: SSL7 forms five H-bonds with a region of β-sheet on the MG5 domain, spanning H511C5-E516C5.
source: While the C5-SSL7 structure reveals a shallow binding site involving a series of five H-bonds between SSL7 and a region of β-sheet on the MG5 domain, spanning H511C5-E516C5 (Laursen et al., 2010), here we show that K92 is wedged between the MG1 and MG5 domains, inducing a re-orientation of the side chain of H511C5 and forming a backbone H-bond with F510C5.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural work, supported by citation.

claim: K92 is wedged between the MG1 and MG5 domains, inducing a re-orientation of the side chain of H511C5 and forming a backbone H-bond with F510C5.
source: While the C5-SSL7 structure reveals a shallow binding site involving a series of five H-bonds between SSL7 and a region of β-sheet on the MG5 domain, spanning H511C5-E516C5 (Laursen et al., 2010), here we show that K92 is wedged between the MG1 and MG5 domains, inducing a re-orientation of the side chain of H511C5 and forming a backbone H-bond with F510C5.
evidence: This is derived from the crystal structure.

claim: SSL7 is a full, or occasional partial, antagonist of both the AP and CP.
source: When comparing K92 and SSL7, the small changes observed in the binding pose achieve different allosteric effects; SSL7, either in isolation or in complex with its second ligand IgA, is full, or occasional partial, antagonist of both the AP and CP (Bestebroer et al., 2010; Laursen et al., 2010), while K92 is a selective partial antagonist of the AP.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: In the C5-K92 complex, the C-terminus of the C5a domain adopts a helical conformation, burying the Bb-cleavage site (R751).
source: Inspection of the C5a anaphylatoxin domain reveals that the C-terminus of the C5a domain in the C5-K92 complex adopts a helical conformation, which is analogous to the C5-OmCI-RaCI complex, burying the Bb-cleavage site (R751).
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis.

claim: In the C5-K8 complex, only sparse continuous electron density was observed for the linker extending from MG6 to C5a, possibly suggesting its R751 scissile bond is more exposed.
source: In other C5 structures (including C5-apo and C5-CVF), this linker adopts an extended conformation following an unstructured loop and only sparse continuous electron density was observed for the linker extending from MG6 to C5a in the C5-K8 complex, possibly suggesting its R751 scissile bond is more exposed.
evidence: This is derived from structural analysis and comparison.

claim: When the MG5 domains in the C5-K92 complex and the C5-apo structure are superimposed, a slight twist can be observed in the MG1 domain, resulting in a significant rotational movement of the C5 α-chain.
source: When the MG5 domains in the C5-K92 complex and the C5-apo structure are superimposed (Figure 4C), a slight twist can be observed in the MG1 domain, caused by the binding of K92 and resulting in a significant rotational movement of the C5 α-chain.
evidence: This is derived from structural comparison.

claim: A similar conformational change to that induced by K92 results from the binding of OmCI and RaCI, and to some extent K8.
source: A similar conformational change results from the binding of OmCI and RaCI, and to some extent K8, as these structures are virtually superimposable.
evidence: This is derived from structural comparison.

claim: CVF can form a highly stable C3/C5 convertase following incubation with factor D and factor B in the presence of Mg2+.
source: CVF can form a highly stable C3/C5 convertase, following incubation with factor D and factor B in the presence of Mg2+ (Vogel and Müller-Eberhard, 1982), which may offer a surrogate model for C5 convertase (Laursen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: When superimposing C5-K92 and C5-CVF complexes, C5 does not adopt a similar conformation as when bound by K92 and K8.
source: When superimposing C5-K92 and C5-CVF (PDB accession code 3PVM) complexes, C5 does not adopt a similar conformation as when bound by K92 and K8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), potentially indicating both knob domains stabilise a different C5 conformation than binds the C5 convertase.
evidence: This is derived from structural comparison and inference.

claim: Both K92 and K8 potentially stabilise a different C5 conformation than binds the C5 convertase.
source: When superimposing C5-K92 and C5-CVF (PDB accession code 3PVM) complexes, C5 does not adopt a similar conformation as when bound by K92 and K8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), potentially indicating both knob domains stabilise a different C5 conformation than binds the C5 convertase.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: The C5-CVF crystal structure reveals that CVF and C5 align perfectly to create a mirror image complex.
source: When considering the organisation of the C5 convertases, the C5-CVF crystal structure reveals that CVF and C5 align perfectly to create a mirror image complex, with a conformational change in the C5 convertase site at arginine 751, potentially placing C5a within range of the catalytic unit of the MG7-associated convertase complex, offering a surrogate model for C5 convertase activation (Laursen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural work, supported by citation.

claim: K92 is not an orthosteric inhibitor of either the CP or the AP convertase.
source: We have shown that K92 is not an orthosteric inhibitor of either the CP or the AP convertase, thereby precluding binding of the convertase to a cleft between the MG1–MG5 domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing partial antagonism.

claim: The K92 epitope is compatible with the CVF model for C5 activation.
source: As the K92 epitope is entirely contained within the SSL7 binding site, this is compatible with the CVF model for C5 activation, with a co-crystal structure of the ternary complex of C5, CVF, and SSL7 (PDB accession code 3PRX6), demonstrating that the CVF and SSL7 binding sites do not cross block.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and prior structural knowledge.

claim: Binding of K8 to the MG8 domain would not appear to sterically block the catalytic unit.
source: Also consistent with the CVF model for C5 activation, binding of K8 to the MG8 domain would not appear to sterically block the catalytic unit.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: SEC-MALLS confirmed that the increases in molecular weight of the C5-knob domain complexes were consistent throughout the elution peaks.
source: SEC-MALLS confirmed that the increases in molecular weight of the complexes were consistent throughout the elution peaks (Supplementary file 1, Table 3.1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data.

claim: For the C5-knob domain complexes, the scattering curves showed slight increases in both the RG and solute volume.
source: For the complexes, the scattering curves showed slight increases in both the RG and solute volume (Supplementary file 1, Table 3.1), with the C5-K8 complex showing the largest change and C5-K149 the smallest change, corresponding with the absence of function and suggesting K149 binds peripherally to a conformation closely resembling C5-apo.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data.

claim: The C5-K8 complex showed the largest change in RG and solute volume.
source: For the complexes, the scattering curves showed slight increases in both the RG and solute volume (Supplementary file 1, Table 3.1), with the C5-K8 complex showing the largest change and C5-K149 the smallest change, corresponding with the absence of function and suggesting K149 binds peripherally to a conformation closely resembling C5-apo.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data.

claim: C5-K149 showed the smallest change in RG and solute volume, suggesting K149 binds peripherally to a conformation closely resembling C5-apo.
source: For the complexes, the scattering curves showed slight increases in both the RG and solute volume (Supplementary file 1, Table 3.1), with the C5-K8 complex showing the largest change and C5-K149 the smallest change, corresponding with the absence of function and suggesting K149 binds peripherally to a conformation closely resembling C5-apo.
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS data and functional data.

claim: For K92 and K57, the discrepancies observed in the mid s range indicate an overall change in flexibility of C5 upon binding of these peptides.
source: For K92 and K57, the discrepancies observed in the mid s range indicate an overall change in flexibility of C5 upon binding of these peptides, and this tuning of dynamics may contribute to their mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS data.

claim: Tuning of dynamics may contribute to the mechanism of K92 and K57.
source: For K92 and K57, the discrepancies observed in the mid s range indicate an overall change in flexibility of C5 upon binding of these peptides, and this tuning of dynamics may contribute to their mechanism.
evidence: This is speculative inference from SAXS data.

claim: C5 adopts a more elongated conformation in solution than the crystal structure would suggest.
source: Consistent with earlier observations (Fredslund et al., 2008), comparison of the C5-apo experimental data with the theoretical scattering curve revealed discrepancies in the lowest angle range, indicating C5 adopts a more elongated conformation in solution than the crystal structure would suggest (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data and comparison to crystal structure.

claim: Normal mode analysis using SREFLEX improved the fit of the C5 model to SAXS data from χ2 >13 to 1.55.
source: To better approximate C5 in solution, we performed a normal mode model analysis (NMA) using SREFLEX (Panjkovich and Svergun, 2016) and found that elongation of the C5 model improved the χ2 from >13 to 1.55.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling of SAXS data.

claim: The fit of the C5-K92 complex to SAXS data was improved by NMA from an initial χ² of >20 to 2.5.
source: The fit of the C5-K92 complex was also markedly improved by the NMA, whereby elongation and incorporation of the peptide improved the model from an initial χ² of >20, to 2.5 (with an overall root mean square [RMS] of 3.8 in both cases).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling of SAXS data.

claim: The absence of the C345c domain in the C5-K8 co-crystal structure was problematic for fitting SAXS data.
source: When using the C5-K8 co-crystal structure for fitting of the C5-K8 SAXS data, the absence of the C345c domain was problematic.
evidence: This is a methodological observation from SAXS analysis.

claim: A hybrid model with the C345c domain reinstated for C5-K8 initially produced a poor fit (χ²=75) but was improved to χ²=4.1 after refinement.
source: The generation of a hybrid model where the C345c domain was reinstated initially produced a poor fit (χ²=75). A restrained rigid body analysis of this model followed by NMA refinement allowed us to significantly reduce the discrepancy to χ²=4.1 indicating an overall acceptable fit.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling of SAXS data.

claim: K8 may induce additional flexibility to the C345c region.
source: The χ² value is still somewhat larger than those observed for the other complexes, which may suggest an increased flexibility around the C345c linker. This result correlates with the absence of clear electron density for the C345c domain in the crystal structure. The latter may be a consequence of K8 inducing additional flexibility to this region, which again could contribute to the efficacy of the peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS and crystallographic data.

claim: Increased flexibility around the C345c linker could contribute to the efficacy of K8.
source: The χ² value is still somewhat larger than those observed for the other complexes, which may suggest an increased flexibility around the C345c linker. This result correlates with the absence of clear electron density for the C345c domain in the crystal structure. The latter may be a consequence of K8 inducing additional flexibility to this region, which again could contribute to the efficacy of the peptide.
evidence: This is speculative inference from SAXS and crystallographic data.

claim: The discrepancies between the crystal structures and the solution scattering data indicate that the constraints of the crystal lattice may impede the detection of more subtle, global changes.
source: The discrepancies between the crystal structures and the solution scattering data indicate that while permitting elucidation of the molecular interaction of the epitopes, the constraints of the crystal lattice may impede the detection of more subtle, global changes, leading to underestimation of the conformational changes induced by the peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of crystallographic and SAXS data.

claim: For C5-K8, the sole protected region of C5 corresponded to the epitope on the MG8 domain (L1380C5-E1387C5).
source: For C5-K8, the sole protected region of C5 corresponded to the epitope on the MG8 domain (L1380C5-E1387C5), although the interface was not entirely defined (Figure 6A, see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, Table 3.2).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: For C5-K8, the neighbouring C5d domain becomes more solvent exposed, suggesting K8 is affecting the dynamics of this domain.
source: Additional conformational changes were observed in the neighbouring C5d domain which becomes more solvent exposed, suggesting K8 is affecting the dynamics of this domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and inferred from the changes observed.

claim: For the C5-K92 complex, there was protection of the C5 residues located in the epitope between the MG1 and MG5 domains (H70C5-L85C5).
source: For the C5-K92 complex, consistent with the crystal structure, there was protection of the C5 residues located in the epitope between the MG1 and MG5 domains (H70C5-L85C5), shown in Figure 6C.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: For C5-K92, there were effects distal to the K92 binding site, notably in C5d (I1169C5-F1227C5) and neighbouring CUB domain (L1303C5-L1346C5), indicating a K92-induced conformational change.
source: There were also effects distal to the K92 binding site, notably in C5d (I1169C5-F1227C5) and neighbouring CUB domain (L1303C5-L1346C5), indicating a K92-induced conformational change.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: For C5-K92, the allosteric network can be visualised by changes in solvent exposure which propagate from the K92 epitope through MG2 domain (L126C5-V145C5) and into the C5d and CUB domains.
source: Interestingly, the allosteric network can be visualised by changes in solvent exposure which propagate from the K92 epitope through MG2 domain (L126C5-V145C5) and into the C5d and CUB domains.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: For the C5-K57 complex, clear protection was observed in the MG5 domain, immediately adjacent to the K92 epitope (N483C5-L540C5).
source: For the C5-K57 complex, the absence of a co-crystal structure meant we had no prior knowledge of the K57 epitope. However, clear protection was observed in the MG5 domain, immediately adjacent to the K92 epitope (N483C5-L540C5), with sparse areas of increased solvent exposure located in the MG6 (Q572C5-L590C5), MG8 (L1379C5-A1388C5), and C5d (K1048C5-Y1064C5) domains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: For C5-K57, a single protected peptide was present in the CUB domain (G951C5-L967C5), suggesting the K57 epitope may be on either the MG5 or CUB domains.
source: A single protected peptide was also present in the CUB domain (G951C5-L967C5), suggesting the K57 epitope may be on either the MG5 or CUB domains.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS data.

claim: There was little protection or deprotection of proteolytic fragments of the C5a domain in any of the complexes.
source: There was little protection or deprotection of proteolytic fragments of the C5a domain in any of the complexes; we therefore propose that the knob domain peptides do not act by inducing conformational changes which shield the scissile arginine bond.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: The knob domain peptides do not act by inducing conformational changes which shield the scissile arginine bond.
source: There was little protection or deprotection of proteolytic fragments of the C5a domain in any of the complexes; we therefore propose that the knob domain peptides do not act by inducing conformational changes which shield the scissile arginine bond.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS data.

claim: The knob domain peptides likely affect more global changes in C5 which lower the affinity for C3b or the C5 convertases.
source: Taken in the context of the other changes, notably in the C5d and CUB domains, it is more probable that they affect more global changes in C5 which lower the affinity for C3b or the C5 convertases.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS and structural data.

claim: The HDX-MS data are in good agreement with the crystallographic data.
source: The HDX-MS data are in good agreement with our crystallographic data, with the K8 and K92 epitopes defined as clear areas of solvent protection.
evidence: This is a comparison of two experimental methods.

claim: The conformational change in the C5d domain evident in the crystal structures also appears to manifest in solution in response to binding of the knob domains.
source: The conformational change in the C5d domain and significant rotational moment of the C5 α-chain, which were evident upon alignment of the MG1 domain of apo C5 with the C5-K8 and C5-K92 co-crystal structures, also appears to manifest in solution in response to binding of the knob domains.
evidence: This is supported by both crystallographic and HDX-MS data.

claim: K8 did not bind C5b but could bind C5b-6.
source: By SPR, K8 did not bind C5b but could C5b-6.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data.

claim: K57, K92, and K149 all bound C5b and C5b-6.
source: However, K57, K92, and K149 all bound C5b and C5b-6 (Supplementary file 1 Table 4.2).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data.

claim: K57, K92, and K149 bound C5b within twofold of their previously published affinities for C5, except for K149 which displayed threefold higher affinity for both C5b and C5b-6.
source: For C5b, this was within twofold of their previously published affinities for C5 (17.8 nM for K8, 1.4 nM for K57, and <0.6 nM for K92; Macpherson et al., 2020), except for K149, which displayed threefold higher affinity for both C5b and C5b-6 than previously reported for C5 (15.5 nM; Macpherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data and comparison to prior work.

claim: K92 exhibited lower affinity for C5b-6 complex than C5, binding the complex at 6.7 nM, relative to <0.6 nM for C5 alone.
source: K92 did exhibit lower affinity for C5b-6 complex than C5, binding the complex at 6.7 nM, relative to <0.6 nM for C5 alone.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data.

claim: The CUB domain is significantly altered in C5b.
source: As the CUB domain is significantly altered in C5b, this increases the likelihood that, of the two protected regions identified by HDX-MS, the K57 epitope is on the MG5 domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C5b structure.

claim: The K57 epitope is likely on the MG5 domain.
source: As the CUB domain is significantly altered in C5b, this increases the likelihood that, of the two protected regions identified by HDX-MS, the K57 epitope is on the MG5 domain.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS data and binding to C5b.

claim: K57 is a novel C5 inhibitor.
source: Functional characterisation at the level of individual complement pathways identified K57 as a novel C5 inhibitor, which is a fully efficacious inhibitor of the terminal pathway in response to both CP and AP activation, and a potential therapeutic candidate for complement-mediated disorders, such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by functional assays.

claim: K57 is a potential therapeutic candidate for complement-mediated disorders, such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
source: Functional characterisation at the level of individual complement pathways identified K57 as a novel C5 inhibitor, which is a fully efficacious inhibitor of the terminal pathway in response to both CP and AP activation, and a potential therapeutic candidate for complement-mediated disorders, such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing efficacy.

claim: K149 may be of considerable value as a non-inhibitory reagent for the detection of native C5.
source: Additionally, the discovery of K149 as a 'silent binder' of C5 may be of considerable value as a non-inhibitory reagent for the detection of native C5 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and functional data.

claim: This is the first reported example of complement pathway-specific inhibition through C5.
source: K92 achieved selective inhibition of the AP through a non-competitive mechanism (Figure 1). To our knowledge, this is the first reported example of complement pathway-specific inhibition through C5 and the first experimental evidence reported for mechanistic differences between the AP and CP C5 convertases.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: This is the first experimental evidence reported for mechanistic differences between the AP and CP C5 convertases.
source: K92 achieved selective inhibition of the AP through a non-competitive mechanism (Figure 1). To our knowledge, this is the first reported example of complement pathway-specific inhibition through C5 and the first experimental evidence reported for mechanistic differences between the AP and CP C5 convertases.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Selective inhibition of C5-cleavage by the AP C5-convertase may partially preserve serum bactericidal activity, thereby lowering the risk of meningococcal disease.
source: Selective inhibition of C5-cleavage by the AP C5-convertase, and not the CP C5-convertase, may partially preserve serum bactericidal activity, thereby lowering the risk of meningococcal disease.
evidence: This is speculative inference about potential therapeutic benefits.

claim: Complete inhibition of the terminal pathway has been shown to increase the susceptibility of eculizumab patients to Neisseria meningitidis infections.
source: Complete inhibition of the terminal pathway has been shown to increase the susceptibility of eculizumab patients to Neisseria meningitidis infections (McNamara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Knob domains can be raised to inhibit flat surfaces involved in protein–protein interactions, which might not offer binding sites for orthosteric small molecules.
source: This may mean that knob domains can be raised to inhibit flat surfaces involved in protein–protein interactions, which might not offer binding sites for orthosteric small molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing K8 binding to a planar epitope.
